stem: On what date was Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany?

options.rationale: Correct: by President Hindenburg.

options.content: 9 November 1923

options.content: 5 March 1933
options.rationale: This was the date of the last multi-party election.

options.content: 2 August 1934
options.rationale: This was the day Hindenburg died.

explanation: Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor on **30 January 1933**.

stem: What did the Nazis mean by 'Lebensraum'?

options.content: Land in Eastern Europe for Germans

stem: Why did the Nazis have little electoral success between 1924 and 1929?

options.content: The party was banned until 1929
options.rationale: The ban was lifted and the party refounded in 1925.

options.content: Germany was more prosperous and stable
options.rationale: Correct: few voters were drawn to extremists.

options.content: Hitler was in prison throughout these years
options.rationale: He was released in December 1924.

options.content: Women were not allowed to vote until 1930
options.rationale: Women had voted since 1919.

explanation: Under Stresemann the economy recovered, so **few voters wanted extreme solutions**.

stem: How did Chancellor Brüning govern Germany from 1930?

options.content: With a coalition of the Nazis and the Communists
options.rationale: The two parties were bitter enemies.

options.content: As head of a military government after a coup
options.rationale: There was no coup in 1930.

options.content: By holding a referendum on every important law
options.rationale: Laws were made by decree, not referendums.

options.content: By presidential decree under Article 48
options.rationale: Correct: he had no Reichstag majority.

explanation: **Brüning** relied on Hindenburg's emergency decrees, so democracy was already weakened.

stem: Why did Papen and Hindenburg agree to make Hitler Chancellor in January 1933?

options.rationale: He made no such promise.

stem: Describe the main ideas of the Nazi Party in the 1920s.

points.description: Destroy the Treaty of Versailles / unite all Germans in a Greater Germany.
Racism: Aryan master race; anti-Semitism, Jews excluded from citizenship.
Lebensraum: expansion into Eastern Europe.
Opposition to democracy and communism; one strong leader / 'socialist' promises to workers and small traders.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Nazis wanted to destroy the Treaty of Versailles and unite all German-speakers in a Greater Germany. They believed Germans were an Aryan master race and blamed Jews for Germany's problems, saying Jews should not be citizens. They wanted Lebensraum, living space in Eastern Europe. They rejected democracy and communism and wanted one strong leader, and they made 'socialist' promises to workers and small traders.

stem: Explain why the Munich Putsch turned out to be useful to Hitler.

points.description: Identifies the trial as publicity.
Explains that newspapers reported his speeches nationally, making him famous among nationalists.
Identifies the change of tactics / Mein Kampf.
Explains that he decided to win power legally through elections and set out his ideas in Mein Kampf.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: His trial gave Hitler a national platform: newspapers across Germany reported his attacks on the republic and Versailles, and sympathetic judges gave him a light sentence. In prison he wrote Mein Kampf and decided to change tactics, winning power legally through elections rather than by force, which was the strategy that eventually succeeded.

hints: What happened after the putsch failed?

stem: Explain why support for the Nazis grew between 1929 and 1932.

points.description: Identifies the Depression / unemployment.
Explains that over six million unemployed and fearful middle classes turned to a party promising work and strong action.
Identifies fear of communism.
Explains that the rising KPD vote drove business, farmers and the middle classes to the Nazis as a barrier.
Identifies propaganda and Hitler's appeal.
Explains that Goebbels' methods and Hitler's image as a strong leader above party quarrels reached many groups.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Depression was the main reason. Unemployment rose to over six million, and the middle classes feared a repeat of 1923, so many turned to a party that promised work and strong action. Fear of communism also helped: as the Communist vote rose, business leaders, farmers and the middle classes saw the Nazis as a barrier against revolution. Nazi propaganda, organised by Goebbels with rallies, posters and films, presented Hitler as a strong leader above the quarrelling parties who had something to offer every group.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a description in words of a Nazi election poster of the kind used in 1932 (described in words; invented for this question)

> A crowd of thin, grey-faced men and women with tired eyes stands in a long line. Across the top in large letters: 'Our last hope'. Below, in smaller letters, the name of the party's leader.

**Source B** — an extract from the memoirs of a fictional Berlin shopkeeper, published in 1955 (invented for this question)

> I voted for them in 1932. I was not a party man and cared little for their talk about race. My shop was failing, my son had no work, and every week there was fighting in the street between the Reds and the Brownshirts. Hitler at least seemed to know what he wanted. I thought the old gentlemen around Hindenburg would keep him in order.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the message of Source A?

points.description: Ordinary Germans are suffering / desperate in the Depression.
The Nazis (Hitler) are the only hope of rescue.

parts.label: (b)

points.description: Supports: economic despair (failing shop, unemployed son) matches the poster's suffering crowd.
Supports: Hitler seen as a strong leader / hope.

Differs: B shows a voter who ignored Nazi racial ideas and trusted conservatives to control Hitler.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How useful are these sources for explaining the rise of the Nazis? Use the sources and your own knowledge.

points.description: A: useful for Nazi propaganda methods and targeting of the unemployed.
A: shows what the Nazis wanted voters to think, not why they voted.
B: useful for one voter's motives (economy, fear of communism, Hitler's appeal).
B: written in 1955, after the war: may play down support for Nazi ideas (hindsight/self-justification).
Own knowledge: election figures 1928-32; Papen and Hindenburg's deal.
Supported judgement.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A is useful as evidence of Nazi propaganda: it targeted the unemployed and presented the party as the last hope, which matches Goebbels' methods. But it shows only what the Nazis wanted voters to believe. Source B is useful because it gives a voter's own reasons: economic ruin, fear of communist street fighting and Hitler's image as a strong leader. It also mentions the conservatives around Hindenburg, which my own knowledge confirms were decisive in January 1933. However, it was written in 1955, after the war, and the shopkeeper may play down his support for Nazi ideas to excuse himself. Together, and checked against the rise from 2.6% in 1928 to 37.3% in 1932, the sources are useful but must be used with care.

parts.explanation: Usefulness from content, provenance and own knowledge.

hints: Compare why each source was produced and when.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The Depression was vital. Before 1929 the Nazis were a fringe party with 2.6% of the vote. Once unemployment rose to over six million, their vote rose to 18.3% in 1930 and 37.3% in July 1932. The Depression also broke parliamentary government: from 1930 Brüning ruled by decree, and fear of the growing Communist Party pushed business and the middle classes towards the Nazis.

However, other parties also gained from the crisis, and the Nazis gained most because of their own methods. Goebbels' propaganda, the SA's show of strength and Hitler's image as a strong leader allowed them to appeal to many groups at once.

The final step was not caused by voters at all. The Nazi vote fell in November 1932, but Papen, seeking revenge on Schleicher, persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler, believing the conservatives could control him.

I largely agree. Without the Depression Hitler would never have been in a position to be considered for Chancellor, but the timing and manner of his appointment were decided by a small group of conservative politicians.

parts.explanation: Levels: both sides with a supported judgement for the top level.

hints: In (b), compare the Depression with Nazi methods and the conservatives' deal.
